name: Yusuf Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign, and your answers here are confidential. You can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 43, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I changed into this trade recently, and I still need more help and checking than the others. I spend a lot of the day carrying materials, preparing runs and fitting parts under supervision; today I mixed up two labels and the senior worker caught it before testing. I like seeing a room take shape, but it's hard being keen and still being the slow one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits around that work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Amina does clothing repairs, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I'm on low pay with three weeks of expenses saved and few electrical firms nearby. I use AI every day to quiz myself on what I've learned, then check with the course book or supervisor; enthusiasm isn't a qualification. I think people changing trades should have funded learning and decent protection, not a bill for every attempt to keep working.

say: I'd welcome **tidier job notes** without needing the technology story to become dramatic.
I'd keep the study helper while asking for **real-person learning** time for juniors too.
think: Even unchanged work leaves me **slow and low paid**, with little room before the mortgage payment.
Three weeks of **savings** cannot become a comfortable buffer simply because the AI story stays quiet.
do: Switch my phone to the **basic tariff** when the contract allows it, after comparing the actual bill.
Continue **supervised work** and checked study questions while protecting the children's homework time.
Ask my brother for one **school pickup** weekly without assuming he can agree.
feel: **Anxious** about the mortgage calendar, despite having work and feeling no fear of the study app.
S0.quote: My study app can't turn three weeks of savings into a fourth.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** supports study rather than independent authority; he checks uncertain answers with the supervisor before practical work.
The **family request** is specific and unconfirmed, while current anxiety follows low wages and a thin mortgage buffer.

steps.text: Switch the phone to a cheaper basic tariff when the contract allows
Continue supervised electrical work and checked evening study questions
Ask the brother for one agreed school pickup each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I could live with a future where the cleverest new thing was a tidier job note. I'd still use my little study helper, because remembering the basics matters to me. I'd ask that juniors got time with a real person as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about a mortgage payment arriving before enough wage had landed. The job could carry on exactly as it was and I'd still be slow, low paid and short of spare money. My study app can't turn three weeks of savings into a fourth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd compare the phone bills and switch my own plan to the cheaper basic tariff when the contract allowed it. In the plateau's first year I'd keep doing supervised work and use the checked study questions in the evening, stopping when the children needed homework help. I'd ask my brother for one school pickup a week so Amina and I weren't always juggling jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, and a little embarrassed that a steady job doesn't mean a steady feeling. I wouldn't be frightened of the app. I'd be watching the mortgage date on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask your brother to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether one agreed afternoon was possible, not assume family had to drop everything. If my brother couldn't do it, we'd keep the existing arrangement. I wouldn't build paid work plans around an answer I hadn't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a study answer disagreed with the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the question to the supervisor before using it at work. The tool can help me practise words, but I don't decide a circuit is safe because a chat box agrees with me. I'm still learning the trade.

say: I'd ask the firm to count **learning time** before adding appointments to a faster schedule.
I'd back a **shared paid-training request** so juniors don't each hide the same basic question.
think: Less senior time could slow my **practical learning**, keeping me on low pay even while repair work remains.
My **paid hours** could shrink if easier preparation tasks are squeezed, despite quick use of a study tool.
do: Ask the **association contact** for named paid supervised practice without reducing wages.
Try the proven **job-note assistant** only in paid time, with senior checks on any record used at work.
Switch to the cheaper **phone tariff** when the contract permits.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and slow progress, while impatient to learn with support that doesn't consume family time.
S1.quote: I can use a study tool quickly and still be a beginner on site.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **software fluency** from practical competence and sees task compression as a possible threat to his own paid hours.
The **shared request** specifies supervision, paid time and maintained wages, rather than treating a video invitation as funded practical development.

steps.text: Support the association request for named paid supervised practice without wage cuts
Try the job-note assistant only in paid time with senior checks
Switch to the cheaper phone tariff when the contract permits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should count learning time before it counts extra appointments. A software plan might be quick, but I still need someone to show me what a good connection looks like. I'd back a shared request for paid training rather than make every junior hide the same question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands still have useful work, but I could be left with fewer chances to practise if senior workers were pushed through more visits. Then I'd stay on the low wage for longer or lose paid hours when the easy preparation tasks got squeezed. I can use a study tool quickly and still be a beginner on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the crew's workers' association contact to include paid supervised practice in its request to the owner. During the first year I'd try the firm's proven job-note assistant only on paid time, with the senior worker checking anything used on site. I'd also switch to the cheaper phone tariff when allowed, because waiting for better pay wasn't a household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and impatient to learn, with a real worry that my hours could shrink. I'd still want to try the tool. What bothers me is a learning plan that only works if I donate evenings my family needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an acceptable paid practice place include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a named senior person and one paid session each week on jobs I was allowed to practise. I'd want the owner to say those hours wouldn't reduce my wage. I wouldn't call an invitation to watch a video a paid training place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you felt pressured to stop asking basic questions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down the question and bring it to the association contact rather than quietly guessing. I'm not too old to need a check. I don't want being eager to look like being ready for work I can't yet do safely.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 and ask who pays for the learning gap.
I'd remind the crew that a junior with a **mortgage** cannot live on enthusiasm alone.
think: I expect a **large junior-hours cut** as the firm prepares for capable hands-on machines.
My wage covers a real **mortgage share**, and my partner's clothing work cannot instantly replace it.
do: Ask the association to check **support eligibility** and contact the lender before missing a payment.
Enroll in practical **training** before 2028 only with funded fees and maintained paid hours.
Apply after 2028 for posted **supervised repair jobs**, checking written wages, travel costs and duties within actual competence.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss, with practical actions that do not remove sleepless account-checking.
S2.quote: A junior with a mortgage can't live on being keen.
fieldNote: His **alarm** follows an expected large wage loss and explicit disrupted sleep, while the action plan prevents a claim of helpless panic.
He keeps **support, funding and vacancies** conditional and refuses to claim the qualifications needed for unsupervised work.

steps.text: Check support eligibility and ask the lender about actual mortgage options
Enroll in practical training only with funded fees and maintained paid hours
Apply after 2028 for posted supervised repair jobs covering household needs after travel in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew not to confuse the 2028 thinking change with robots following around 2031. I'd use whatever learning time came before both dates, but I'd ask who paid for it. A junior with a mortgage can't live on being keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would expect the firm to cut a large share of junior hours as it prepared for machines that could do the hands-on work too. My small wage still pays a real part of our mortgage, and Amina's clothing repairs couldn't just expand overnight. I'd be awake making sums I didn't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the association contact to help check actual support eligibility and talk to the mortgage lender before missing a payment. I'd enroll in a practical course before 2028 only if fees were funded and my paid hours were maintained. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted supervised repair jobs, comparing the written wage and travel with what the household needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect to lose a big part of the wage, and the date feels close. I'd be doing things, not sitting still. But I can imagine checking the account at two in the morning while everyone else sleeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner before contacting the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Amina the amount I feared losing, not just say that technology was changing. We'd put the mortgage and essential bills on paper and ask the lender what options actually existed. I wouldn't tell the children that a possible payment arrangement was already approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for an unsupervised maintenance role if it paid more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what supervised training came with the vacancy and what the hours actually paid. I couldn't turn a study app or a vocational certificate into experience I don't have. The right next job would have to be one I could actually do with checks.

say: I'd ask for **paid learning** that leads to real competence rather than reassurance repeated until 2031.
I'd support association requests for **skilled supervision**, keeping the later hands-on robot date in view.
think: More time could let me become **competent** before the hardest changes to practical electrical work.
Today's **children and mortgage** still make me anxious because the household buffer remains thin.
do: Maintain the shared **paid-practice request** and cut the phone tariff when possible.
Take practical **training** before 2031 only with covered fees, protected paid hours and maintained wages.
Apply after 2031 for posted **supervised roles** offering better pay after travel and matching completed skills.
feel: **Anxious** about present money, with more hope and less hurry around practical learning.
S3.quote: I wouldn't have more money in the bank just because AGI arrived later.
fieldNote: The **longer preparation** improves his learning prospects without removing the baseline money worries shared across the interview.
He protects **family time and wages**, checking actual completed tasks and pay rather than collecting unpaid courses indefinitely.

steps.text: Maintain the association request for named paid supervised practice
Cut the phone tariff when the current contract allows
Take practical training only with covered fees, protected paid hours and maintained wages
Apply for supervised roles matching completed skills and improving pay after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should mean paid learning that leads somewhere, not the same reassuring message repeated until 2031. I'd keep asking through the association for time beside a skilled worker. The robots around 2034 would still reach hands-on work in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have a better chance to become competent before the hardest change. But I would still be short of money now, with two children and a mortgage that didn't move to a later date. I'd be anxious about the household even if I was more hopeful about learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep supporting the shared request for named paid practice and make the phone-tariff cut when possible. I'd take practical training before 2031 only if fees were covered and paid hours protected. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for posted supervised roles with better pay after travel, using only the skills I'd actually completed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less hurried about becoming useful. I'd have more time to make mistakes with somebody checking me, which is what learning needs. I wouldn't have more money in the bank just because AGI arrived later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect family time while learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't fill all five years with unpaid courses. We'd compare the actual evening hours with the children's needs and only accept funded practical training that preserved my wage. I want them to see me learning, not only see the back of my head over another screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the extra years were improving your position?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at whether I was allowed to do more checked tasks correctly and whether that brought better pay. If neither changed, I'd ask the association about actual posted vacancies earlier. Hope needs a real job attached before I rely on it.

say: I'd use **a decade's warning** to ask for proper paid adult routes into trade competence now.
I'd reject leaving juniors waiting simply because **2036 and 2039** look far away on a calendar.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I would still need earnings without assuming retirement income or a vanished mortgage.
Today's **low wages and reserve** still worry me, even if the children will be older later.
do: Keep the **association request** active and ask for named paid practice with clear skill targets.
Enroll in practical **training** before 2036 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours.
Apply after 2036 for posted **repair roles** within completed competence and with workable written wages after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about present household money, while more hopeful that time could bring actual competence and better pay.
S4.quote: A long warning isn't paid experience by itself.
fieldNote: He avoids **retirement and children's-income assumptions**, keeping future household resources separate from money he can actually count.
The **annual competence check** uses correctly completed work and wages, with an earlier vacancy search if the same promises repeat.

steps.text: Keep the shared request for named paid supervised practice active
Enroll in practical training only with covered fees and maintained paid hours
Apply for repair roles matching competence and paying enough after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough warning to build proper paid routes for adults learning a trade. I'd still ask for those routes now, while there was time to correct what didn't work. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 shouldn't become an excuse for leaving the juniors waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change and around 56 when the robots followed, still needing earnings unless our real finances said otherwise. I can't assume the children being grown means the mortgage disappears. I would still be anxious today about low wages and only three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the association request active and ask at my review for named paid practice and clear skill targets. I'd enroll in practical training before 2036 only with fees covered and paid hours maintained. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for posted repair roles within my completed competence, checking the written wage after travel before any move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current account, with more room to imagine becoming good at this work. I wouldn't be relaxed simply because the big dates were further away. I'd want the next year's pay and learning to improve in real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the decade from turning into waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check every year which tasks I could now do correctly with the required checks and whether the wage reflected that. If the same promise kept coming back, I'd use actual vacancies to look elsewhere earlier. A long warning isn't paid experience by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what you told the children about their future work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell them to choose a whole life from one technology picture. I'd show them that adults can start learning again and still ask for fair pay. I wouldn't count their future wages as part of my own safety plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose a big part of the wage before I'd learned enough to earn it somewhere else. Paid practical training with fees covered would help, along with someone checking our actual mortgage options rather than promising support. I need a route from being keen to being paid for work I can do safely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the person who learns quickly from a screen. I enjoy the tool, but practical mistakes don't care how confident the answer sounded. I want help becoming good, not a badge for looking adaptable.

headlineQuote: I need a route from being keen to being paid for work I can do safely.
portrait: **Yusuf, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, low pay and practical skills still below the experienced crew's level.
He and **his partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and three weeks of expenses saved near few electrical employers.
His **daily AI study** shows curiosity without replacing supervision; he favours shared requests for paid training and actual household support checks.
Expected major hours loss brings **alarm** in the fast picture; longer preparation improves learning prospects without erasing present money anxiety.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove much of his wage before he gains enough practical skill to earn elsewhere.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** with covered fees would turn willingness into achievable learning.
Help checking actual **mortgage options** would support a plan without assuming assistance is approved.
